bib.title: Tool-to-Agent Retrieval: Bridging Tools and Agents for Scalable LLM Multi-Agent Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Tool-to-Agent Retrieval: Bridging Tools and Agents for Scalable LLM Multi-Agent Systems". Elias Lumer, Faheem Nizar, Anmol Gulati, Pradeep Honaganahalli Basavaraju, Vamse Kumar Subbiah (PricewaterhouseCoopers U.S.A.). arXiv:2511.01854v2 [cs.CL], 4 Nov 2025. It is a preprint, with no venue stated.

COVERAGE: 24,700 of 24,700 chars read (all 10 pages: 7 of body, 3 of references). There are no appendices. I did not run the figure-caption script. Fig. 1 is a diagram of agent-only versus joint retrieval, and its caption is in the extracted text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Embedding tools and their parent agents in one index, then mapping retrieved tools up to their owning agent, beats the baselines at picking the right agent or MCP server.
  number: Recall@5 0.83 vs MCPZero 0.70, ScaleMCP 0.74, Q.Retrieval 0.56, BM25 0.20. nDCG@5 0.46 vs 0.41, 0.40, 0.32, 0.14.
  setup: LiveMCPBench (70 MCP servers, 527 tools, 95 questions), step-wise querying, retrieving agents.
  quote: "Tool-to-Agent Retrieval 0.61 0.77 0.83 0.61 0.49 0.34 0.61 0.56 0.46" (Table 1; MCPZero row "0.44 0.66 0.70 0.45 0.39 0.31 0.45 0.46 0.41")
  where: p.5, Table 1
- Claim: The headline gain is reported as about 18 to 19%, but the paper states the figures inconsistently.
  number: 19.4% Recall@5 and 17.7% nDCG@5 (abstract, conclusion). The contributions list swaps them.
  setup: eight embedding models, "over previous state-of-the-art agent retrievers".
  quote: "achieves consistent improvements of 19.4% in Recall@5 and 17.7% in nDCG@5" (abstract). Contributions: "demonstrating 17.7% (recall@5) and 19.4% (nDCG@5) improvements".
  where: p.1 and p.3. The baseline and relative-versus-absolute basis is never defined.
- Claim: The gain holds across all eight embedding models, including a small open-source one.
  number: Recall@5 ranges from 0.80 to 0.87 against MCPZero's 0.65 to 0.74. Titan v2 goes 0.66 to 0.85, a +28% relative gain. All-MiniLM-L6-v2 gains +13%. Standard deviations are 0.02 (Recall@5) and 0.01 (nDCG@5).
  setup: Table 2, per-embedding comparison against MCPZero only.
  quote: "Recall@5 improved from 0.66 to 0.85, a +28% relative gain), while even the compact All-MiniLM-L6-v2 model achieved a +13% improvement"
  where: p.6, Table 2
- Claim: The lift does not come from tool-level matches alone. Agent-corpus entries also appear in the top-K.
  number: 39.13% of top-K items come from the agent corpus. 34.44% of matched top-K tools also trace back to the agent corpus.
  setup: same benchmark. There is no ablation, such as tool-only versus agent-only versus joint.
  quote: "39.13% of retrieved top-Kitems originating from the agent corpusC A and 34.44% of matched top-Ktools also tracing back toCA"
  where: p.6
- Claim: Listing every tool description in the prompt is too costly, which motivates retrieval.
  number: one MCP server with 26 tools uses over 4,600 tokens.
  setup: a cited figure ([35,38]), not measured in this paper.
  quote: "one MCP server with 26 tools can consume over 4,600 tokens"
  where: p.1
- Claim: The method is a pipeline over a mixed tool and agent index. Retrieve the top N≫K entities, using BM25 plus dense retrieval, and map each tool to its owner via metadata. Deduplicate until K unique agents are found. Decomposing the query into steps and retrieving per step is the primary setting.
  number: none
  setup: Algorithm 1. Tools and agents form a bipartite ownership graph. N and K values for the main runs are not given beyond K∈{1,3,5} in the tables.
  quote: "we first retrieve the topN≫Kentities from the unified tool–agent catalogC, ranked by semantic similarity to the query"
  where: p.4
- Claim: Tool-only retrieval drops agent-level execution context. Agent-first routing hides fine-grained tools, which the paper calls "context dilution".
  number: none (argued, not measured)
  quote: "retrieving tools independently discards important execution context such as authentication, parameter inference, or access policies maintained at the agent level"
  where: p.4
- Claim: Dataset statistics. Each question has about 2.68 steps, 2.82 tools and 1.40 MCP agents.
  quote: "each question spans 2.68 steps and involves 2.82 tools and 1.40 MCP agents"
  where: p.5

LIMITS
- The evaluation is small: one benchmark, 95 questions, 70 servers. There are no confidence intervals or significance tests, and the only variance figure is the standard deviation across embedding models.
- It measures only retrieval of the correct agent, in Recall, mAP and nDCG. No end-to-end task success, latency, token cost or context-size saving is measured, even though context cost is the motivation.
- Table 2 compares against MCPZero only. Table 1's "Tool-to-Agent" Recall@5 of 0.83 does not equal the mean of Table 2's column, which I computed as about 0.85. The MCPZero mean I computed matches Table 1 (0.70). The paper does not explain this.
- The baselines are reproduced by the authors. Q.Retrieval is not defined in the text. The "agent-only baseline" dataset is built by the authors.
- There is no hierarchical (server then tool) pipeline run as its own condition, even though the text frames the method against that approach. MCPZero and ScaleMCP are the nearest comparators.
- The authors concede nothing beyond calling this a "promising direction". There is no limitations section.
- The authors are the same group (PwC) that wrote ScaleMCP, ToolShed, Graph RAG-Tool Fusion and MemTool, so several baselines and citations are self-authored.
- The "architecture-agnostic" claim rests on 8 embedding models and one benchmark.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Lumer et al. 2024, ToolShed (tool knowledge bases and RAG-tool fusion), and Lumer et al. 2025 on ScaleMCP, Graph RAG-Tool Fusion and MemTool.
- Fei et al. 2025, MCP-Zero (hierarchical server-then-tool routing).
- Mo et al. 2025, LiveMCPBench (the benchmark).
- Robertson and Zaragoza 2009 (BM25) and Kuzi et al. 2020 (hybrid lexical plus semantic retrieval).
- Graph approaches: ToolNet (Liu 2024), ControlLLM (Liu 2023), Graph-CoT (Jin 2024), Think-on-Graph (Sun 2024).
- Iterative or decomposed retrieval: ToolReAGT (Braunschweiler 2025), REAPER (Joshi 2024), Re-Invoke (Chen 2024), PLUTO, ProTIP (Anantha 2023).
- Others: AnyTool (Du 2024), ToolRerank (Zheng 2024), Query Rewriting (Ma 2023), EASYTOOL (Yuan 2024).

CODE: Only Algorithm 1 (p.3), in pseudocode. Rank the combined corpus and take the top N. Walk down the list. If the entry is an agent, use it. If it is a tool with a defined owner, use its owner. Otherwise skip it. Add each agent to the set once, and stop at K unique agents.

FIGURES: Fig. 1 (p.2), "Comparison of agent-only retrieval (left) and the proposed Tool-to-Agent Retrieval (right), which embeds tools and agents in a shared vector space to support joint retrieval and traversal." It is useful as a quick diagram of agent-first versus joint-index retrieval, but it adds no numbers.

PROBLEMS
- Table 2 extracts with the two values fused ("0.870.74" means ours 0.87, MCPZero 0.74). I split them by reading the columns.
- There are no embedded instructions.
- The abstract and the contributions list swap which metric gets 19.4% and which gets 17.7%.

ASSESSMENT FOR THE NOTES (plain statement)
- The paper is short (about 7 pages) and a modest preprint. It is on-topic for retrieving tools and agents into the window, and it fits the semantic-versus-hierarchical contrast in 03-tool-design.md. It frames hierarchical (agent-first) routing as suppressing fine-grained matches, and it supports joint tool-and-agent indexing.
- The evidence is thin. Treat the numbers as "on LiveMCPBench, 95 questions, agent-retrieval recall only". Cite the 4,600-token figure as a secondhand citation, not a finding of this paper.
